content: Inhaled antibiotics are frequently utilized to manage persistent airway infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in individuals with cystic fibrosis. These infections contribute significantly to lung damage. Current clinical guidelines recommend the use of inhaled tobramycin for patients aged six years or older who have cystic fibrosis and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections. The primary goal of this treatment is to reduce the bacterial burden in the lungs, thereby mitigating inflammation and slowing the decline in lung function. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of long-term inhaled antibiotic therapy on clinical outcomes, including lung function, frequency of pulmonary exacerbations, nutritional status, quality of life, and adverse events such as drug-related sensitivities and survival rates. The review involved a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, journal handsearches, and conference abstracts. Additionally, ongoing trial registries were examined, with the most recent search conducted on June 28, 2022. Trials were included if they involved cystic fibrosis patients receiving inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for at least three months, with randomized or quasi-randomized treatment allocation and a control group (placebo, no treatment, or another inhaled antibiotic). Two independent reviewers selected the trials, assessed the risk of bias, extracted data, and evaluated the certainty of evidence using the GRADE system. Out of 410 citations, 18 trials involving 3042 participants aged 5 to 45 years met the inclusion criteria. However, due to variability in trial design and reporting, limited data were available for meta-analyses. Eleven trials (1130 participants) compared inhaled antibiotics to placebo or standard treatment over durations ranging from three to 33 months. Five trials (1255 participants) compared different antibiotics, two trials (585 participants) compared different tobramycin regimens, and one trial (90 participants) compared intermittent tobramycin with continuous tobramycin alternating with aztreonam. One trial (18 participants) compared an antibiotic to both placebo and another antibiotic, thus falling into multiple comparison groups. Tobramycin was the most frequently studied antibiotic, featured in 12 trials. Findings for Inhaled Antibiotics Compared to Placebo: Inhaled antibiotics may improve lung function, as measured by various methods (4 trials, 814 participants). They may reduce the frequency of pulmonary exacerbations (risk ratio [RR] 0.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 0.93; 3 trials, 946 participants; low-certainty evidence). Inhaled antibiotics may result in fewer days missed from school or work, a quality-of-life measure (mean difference [MD] -5.30 days, 95% CI -8.59 to -2.01; 1 trial, 245 participants; low-certainty evidence). There was insufficient data to determine effects on nutritional outcomes, and no effect on survival was observed. No significant impact on antibiotic resistance was noted in the two trials included in meta-analyses. Adverse events were uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence, but tinnitus and voice alterations were more frequently reported in the inhaled antibiotics group. The overall certainty of evidence was low for most outcomes due to trial bias and imprecision caused by low event rates. Findings for Comparisons Between Different Antibiotics or Regimens: Eight trials compared different inhaled antibiotics or regimens, with only one trial for each unique comparison. Aztreonam lysine for inhalation likely improved forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted compared to tobramycin (MD -3.40%, 95% CI -6.63 to -0.17; 1 trial, 273 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, differences in endpoint definitions and prolonged tobramycin exposure complicated interpretation. No differences in lung function were observed in other comparisons. Pulmonary exacerbations were measured differently across trials, but aztreonam lysine likely reduced the need for additional antibiotics compared to tobramycin (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.86; 1 trial, 273 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Levofloxacin was associated with fewer hospitalizations due to respiratory exacerbations compared to tobramycin (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.98; 1 trial, 282 participants; high-certainty evidence). Treatment-related adverse events were uncommon but were reported less frequently in the tobramycin group compared to aztreonam lysine and colistimethate. The certainty of evidence for these comparisons varied from low to high, depending on the risk of bias in individual trials. Conclusions: Long-term inhaled anti-pseudomonal antibiotic therapy likely improves lung function and reduces exacerbation rates in cystic fibrosis patients. However, the pooled estimates of benefit are limited. The strongest evidence supports the use of inhaled tobramycin. Further trials with standardized outcome measures are needed to better quantify the benefits. Longer-term studies are also necessary to evaluate the effects of inhaled antibiotics on quality of life, survival, and nutritional outcomes.
